title: Effect of Personalized Email-Based Reminders on Participants’ Timeliness in an Online Education Program: Randomized Controlled Trial
research_question: Do progress-personalized email reminders improve the timeliness of adult online learners more than general schedule-based reminders?
methodology: Thirty-nine professional learners from Ethiopia, Rwanda, and Kenya participating in the OneLearns online program were randomized into an AB-BA reminder design over the course. All participants received weekly email reminders, but personalized reminders additionally reported the participant's observed progress while general reminders only described where the participant should be according to the schedule. Across five months the study sent 585 reminders, comprising 390 general and 195 personalized reminders. A Bayesian mixed-effects logistic regression estimated the probability of being on time while accounting for participant and reminder-time variation.

key_findings.finding: The model-estimated probability of being on time was 14 percentage points higher after personalized reminders than after general reminders, with a 95% credible interval from 3 to 25 percentage points.
In the unadjusted observations, 64.1% of personalized reminders were followed by an on-time state compared with 52.8% of general reminders.
For an average participant at an average reminder time, the model estimated a 70% probability of being on time after personalized reminders and 56% after general reminders.

A relatively small amount of state-specific personalization—telling a learner both expected and observed progress—was sufficient to improve timeliness relative to schedule-only reminders in this sample.
The study had no no-reminder arm, so it estimates the incremental value of personalization over general reminders rather than the causal effect of reminders versus receiving no reminder.
Personalized reminders improved the procrastination problem but did not eliminate it.

limitations: The sample contains only 39 participants, limiting precision and generalizability.
Participants were adult professionals from three East African countries in one specialized online education program.
There was no untreated no-reminder control condition.
The intervention personalizes reminders from current progress but does not learn changing individual reminder preferences.
The study does not evaluate preference drift, obligation-versus-preference selection, or cross-thread work-item state transitions.
It measures timeliness rather than a joint set of omission, repetition, and false-alert outcomes.
The underlying participant data are available only by request from the institution rather than through an unrestricted public download.
raw_claims: The study enrolled 39 active professional learners.
Participants came from Ethiopia, Rwanda, and Kenya.
The intervention sent 585 weekly email reminders over five months.
Personalized reminders included both where the learner should be and the learner's observed current progress.
General reminders described the expected course pace without reporting the learner's observed progress.
Personalized reminders were followed by on-time status in 64.1% of observations, compared with 52.8% after general reminders.
The Bayesian model estimated a 14-percentage-point advantage for personalized reminders.
The 95% credible interval for the estimated advantage was 3 to 25 percentage points.
Personalization improved timeliness but did not eliminate procrastination.
The article supplies a Python program used to convert progress percentages into page numbers.
The study data can be requested from KTH's Registrar's Office.
